stories.title: CISA adds exploited Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to KEV

writeup.what_happened: On 24 November 2026 CISA added three vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. CISA describes CVE-2026-132165 as a Drupal Core flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker abuse the installer (install.php) to reinstall Drupal under specific conditions, taking over the site or running arbitrary code. CVE-2026-131914 is an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw caused by unsafe deserialization in the Idunno AntiCsrf library, which CISA says may be end-of-life. The vulnerability data also lists this product as blowdart anticsrf. CVE-2026-132224 is a flaw in the Optimizely Web Experimentation account signup flow that CISA says lets attackers impersonate customer users, change Project JavaScript and serve malicious script to visitors of affected sites.
writeup.why_it_matters: All three are being exploited, and federal agencies must remediate by 27 November 2026. The AntiCsrf flaw is rated CVSS 9.3 (EPSS 4.3%) and the Drupal flaw has public proof-of-concept code, so any internet-facing Drupal site or .NET web app using AntiCsrf is a direct path to server compromise. The Optimizely issue is a hosted-service supply-chain risk: injected JavaScript can run in your users' browsers without any change to your own servers.
recommended_actions: Inventory internet-facing Drupal sites and apply the vendor's Drupal Core security update now. Until then, block external access to install.php and confirm the installer cannot run on production sites.
Find .NET applications that reference the Idunno or blowdart AntiCsrf package. Move to a supported version or remove the library, since CISA notes it may be end-of-life.
If you use Optimizely Web Experimentation, review Project JavaScript and recent account and user changes for unauthorized edits. Follow Optimizely's mitigation guidance.
On Drupal and IIS hosts, hunt for web server processes spawning shells and for unexpected changes to Drupal settings files, following CISA's forensic triage guidance.
Treat any confirmed exploitation as a full host compromise. Rotate database and application credentials on affected servers.

sources.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
CVE-2026-132224: Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability
CVE-2026-131914: Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability
CVE-2026-132165: Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability

hunting_steps: Identify Drupal and .NET web servers exposed to the internet, and check vulnerability management data for the three CVEs.
Review web server logs for requests to install.php on Drupal sites since mid-November 2026, focusing on successful POST requests from external addresses.
Look for web server worker processes (w3wp, php, httpd, nginx) launching shells or reconnaissance tools.
Check Drupal settings.php files and site directories for unexpected creation or modification.
For Optimizely customers, audit Project JavaScript change history and newly added or changed users in the Optimizely account.

hunting_queries.title: Web server processes spawning shells or recon tools
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","php-cgi.exe","php.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-fpm","apache2") | where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","sh","bash","dash") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, AccountName

hunting_queries.title: Drupal settings.php created or modified
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where FileName =~ "settings.php" and FolderPath has "sites" | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

hunting_queries.title: Devices exposed to the three KEV CVEs
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId in ("CVE-2026-132165","CVE-2026-131914","CVE-2026-132224") | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

stories.title: VMware vCenter SRP authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123890) leads to root; CISA KEV lists it

writeup.what_happened: Rapid7 published an analysis of CVE-2026-123890, a critical (CVSS 9.8) flaw in the VMware vCenter directory service. An unauthenticated attacker who can reach DCE/RPC on TCP 2012 can obtain the session key of a login the attacker starts and complete it as an SSO administrator without the password. Rapid7 reproduced the bypass on vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400 and turned it into root command execution. The chain copied the directory database, took the STS signing key, forged an administrator session, created a local superAdmin account and enabled SSH. SecurityWeek reports that VMware has shipped updates fixing this vCenter bypass along with critical ESX code execution flaws, but the sources do not list fixed builds.
writeup.why_it_matters: vCenter controls the whole virtualization estate, including Windows servers and domain controllers running as VMs, and theft of the STS signing key lets an attacker forge trusted admin sessions even after the bypass is patched. The CVE is in CISA's KEV catalog (no due date given), public proof-of-concept code exists, and EPSS is 5.0%, so treat any vCenter with TCP 2012 reachable from untrusted networks as urgent.
affected_versions: VMware vCenter Server (affected range not stated in the sources; Rapid7 reproduced on vCenter Server Appliance 8.0.2.00400, build 23929136)
recommended_actions: Apply VMware's vCenter updates for CVE-2026-123890 now; take the fixed build numbers from VMware's advisory, because the sources do not state them.
Until patched, use firewall rules to block TCP 2012, 443 and 22 to vCenter from everything except dedicated admin hosts.
Check each vCenter appliance for compromise: unexpected local superAdmin or appliance accounts, SSH or Bash being enabled, and unexplained SSO administrator logins.

If compromise is suspected, treat the STS signing key and directory database as stolen. Rebuild or replace the STS certificates and rotate SSO, root and service account credentials according to VMware guidance.
Review the ESX vulnerabilities fixed in the same release and patch ESX hosts too.

sources.title: Rapid7 Analysis: VMware vCenter SRP Authentication Bypass to Root (CVE-2026-123890)
VMware Updates Patch Critical ESX, vCenter Vulnerabilities

hunting_steps: Inventory every vCenter Server, Cloud Foundation and Telco Cloud deployment and record its build number against VMware's advisory.
Use firewall and NetFlow logs to check which sources can reach vCenter on TCP 2012, and flag any traffic from the internet or from user subnets.
With Defender telemetry, look for managed endpoints opening TCP 2012 connections, which are unusual outside admin tooling.
On each vCenter, review appliance and SSO logs for newly created local accounts, SSH or Bash being turned on, and administrator sessions with no matching interactive login.
Look for SSH sessions to vCenter from unexpected sources, especially when SSH is normally disabled.
Escalate any hit as a possible full virtualization compromise and start credential and STS key rotation.

hunting_queries.title: Endpoints connecting to vCenter directory RPC port TCP 2012
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemotePort == 2012 and ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt") | summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP | order by Connections desc

hunting_queries.title: Inbound connections to TCP 2012 on onboarded devices from public IPs
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where LocalPort == 2012 and ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" | where RemoteIPType == "Public" | summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP | order by Connections desc

hunting_queries.title: Devices flagged by Defender vulnerability management for CVE-2026-123890
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId == "CVE-2026-123890" | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate

stories.title: Check Point Security Management Servers compromised in campaign hitting 22 organizations

writeup.what_happened: BleepingComputer reported on 24 November 2026 that threat actors have compromised about two dozen Check Point Security Management Servers belonging to 22 organizations. According to the report, the attackers exploited multiple vulnerabilities, and the campaign is ongoing. The sources do not name the vulnerabilities, CVE identifiers, affected versions, patches or the threat actor.
writeup.why_it_matters: A management server controls firewall policy, VPN configuration and credentials for every gateway it manages, so a compromise can let attackers change security policy, open access paths or harvest secrets across the network edge. Exploitation is confirmed in the wild and still ongoing. With no vulnerabilities or fixes named yet, the main defenses for now are limiting exposure and checking for signs of compromise.
affected_versions: Check Point Security Management Server (specific versions not stated)
recommended_actions: Confirm that no Check Point Security Management Server or its management ports are reachable from the internet. Restrict access to dedicated admin networks or jump hosts.
Watch Check Point advisories for the exploited vulnerabilities and apply hotfixes as soon as they are published.
Review management server audit logs for unexpected administrator logins, new or changed admin accounts, and policy or VPN configuration changes since early November 2026.
Rotate management administrator credentials and any secrets stored on or pushed from the management server if you see suspicious activity.
Look for unusual outbound connections from the management server and its gateways, and keep a forensic copy before rebuilding any server you suspect.

sources.title: Hackers compromise Check Point Servers in 22 organizations

hunting_steps: Inventory every Check Point Security Management Server and Multi-Domain Server, and confirm with external scans which of them, if any, expose management services to the internet.
In SmartConsole audit logs and Gaia system logs, review administrator logins, focusing on source IPs outside your admin ranges and logins at unusual times.
Check for new administrator accounts, changed permission profiles, new SSH keys and changes to firewall or VPN policy that no change ticket explains.
From the management server and the gateways it manages, hunt for outbound connections to unfamiliar public IP addresses.
On Windows admin workstations that run SmartConsole, look for connections to management ports from unexpected hosts or users.

hunting_queries.title: Inbound public connections to Check Point management ports on onboarded hosts
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" | where LocalPort in (18190, 18191, 18192, 18264, 19009) | where RemoteIPType == "Public" | summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, LocalPort, RemoteIP | order by Connections desc

hunting_queries.title: Workstations and users connecting to Check Point management ports
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemotePort in (18190, 18264, 19009) | summarize Connections = count(), Destinations = make_set(RemoteIP, 50) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName | order by Connections desc

stories.title: Newly formed Inception extortion group runs large-scale vishing campaign against SSO credentials

writeup.what_happened: BleepingComputer reported on 24 November 2026 that a newly formed data extortion group calling itself Inception has been linked to a large-scale voice phishing (vishing) campaign. According to the report, the campaign targets single sign-on (SSO) credentials at multiple global brands and companies. The available reporting does not name the identity providers, the specific social engineering pretexts, the victims, or any indicators of compromise.
writeup.why_it_matters: SSO accounts give access to every application behind the identity provider, including Microsoft 365 and Entra ID-federated SaaS, so one phone call that captures a password and MFA approval can lead straight to data theft and extortion. Exploitation is confirmed in the wild, and no software patch applies; defenses depend on help desk procedures, phishing-resistant MFA and close monitoring of sign-ins and MFA changes. Because the sources give few technical details, defenders should hunt for generic vishing follow-on activity rather than specific indicators.
recommended_actions: Brief the help desk and staff that callers posing as IT or the help desk may ask for SSO credentials, MFA codes or MFA resets, and require out-of-band identity verification before any password or MFA reset.

Enforce phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2 or Windows Hello for Business) for privileged and high-value users and restrict who can register new MFA methods using Conditional Access, for example only from compliant devices or trusted locations.
Review recent MFA method registrations, password resets and new device enrollments, and confirm each was expected with the user.

Hunt for successful sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses or countries shortly after credential or MFA changes, and for bulk data access or downloads in SharePoint, OneDrive and other SSO-connected SaaS applications.
For any suspected compromise, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, reset credentials, and remove attacker-registered MFA methods and devices.

sources.title: New Inception extortion gang launches large-scale vishing campaign

hunting_steps: List MFA or security info registrations and changes from the last 14 days and confirm unexpected ones with the account owners, giving priority to changes made outside business hours or from new IP addresses.
For each account with a recent MFA or password change, review sign-ins in the following 24 hours for new IP addresses, countries or user agents.
Look for accounts with successful sign-ins from several distinct countries or IP addresses in a short period.
Check SSO-connected applications, especially SharePoint, OneDrive and Exchange Online, for unusually high download or file access volume by recently changed accounts.
Correlate any findings with help desk tickets and call logs to find possible social-engineered resets.

hunting_queries.title: Recent MFA / security info registrations and changes
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(14d) | where ActionType has_any ("security info", "StrongAuthentication", "Reset user password", "Register device") | project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, Application | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Accounts signing in successfully from multiple countries in a day
hunting_queries.kql: IdentityLogonEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ActionType == "LogonSuccess" | where isnotempty(Location) | summarize Countries = dcount(Location), CountryList = make_set(Location, 10), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1d) | where Countries > 1 | order by Countries desc

hunting_queries.title: High-volume file downloads in SharePoint/OneDrive per user
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where Application in ("Microsoft SharePoint Online", "Microsoft OneDrive for Business") | where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded", "FileSyncDownloadedFull") | summarize Downloads = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10) by AccountDisplayName, bin(Timestamp, 1h) | where Downloads > 200 | order by Downloads desc

stories.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after attackers accessed customer Kubernetes clusters

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, Rackspace is shutting down its Rackspace Spot cloud platform after a security breach in which attackers gained access to customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets. Customers have until 8 December to migrate their services and download their data. The sources do not describe how the attackers got in, how many customers were affected, or which secrets were exposed.
writeup.why_it_matters: Any credentials, API keys, tokens or certificates stored as secrets in Rackspace Spot clusters should be treated as compromised. Those secrets may grant access to Entra ID applications, Microsoft 365, cloud storage or on-premises systems. The platform is niche, but the impact for affected customers is direct, and the migration deadline is short.
affected_versions: Rackspace Spot (customer Kubernetes clusters and secrets)
recommended_actions: Check whether your organization or any supplier uses Rackspace Spot; if so, inventory every secret stored in those clusters.
Rotate all credentials, API keys, service principal secrets, tokens and certificates that were stored in Spot clusters, starting with those that reach identity providers and production systems.
Review sign-in and audit logs for any service principals or accounts whose secrets were stored in Spot, looking for use from unfamiliar IP addresses or at unusual times.
Migrate workloads and download data before the 8 December deadline, and rebuild workloads from trusted images rather than copying them from the possibly compromised clusters.
Follow Rackspace communications for indicators of compromise or details on the intrusion vector.

sources.title: Rackspace shuts down Spot cloud platform after security breach

hunting_steps: Identify which applications, service principals and accounts had credentials stored as Kubernetes secrets in Rackspace Spot.
In Entra ID sign-in logs and CloudAppEvents, review activity by those identities since the earliest plausible exposure date, looking for new source IPs, new countries or unusual operations.
Look for changes made by those identities to credentials, roles or app consent, which could indicate persistence.
After rotation, confirm that the old credentials no longer succeed and alert on any failed attempts to use them.

hunting_queries.title: Cloud app activity by identities whose secrets may have been in Spot
hunting_queries.kql:
let suspect_ids = dynamic(["replace-with-app-or-account-object-ids"]);
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountObjectId in (suspect_ids) or tostring(RawEventData.AppId) in (suspect_ids)
| summarize Events = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), Countries = make_set(CountryCode, 20), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 50) by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, Application
| order by Events desc

hunting_queries.title: Credential or role changes on service principals in the last 30 days
hunting_queries.kql:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Add service principal credentials", "Update application", "Add app role assignment", "Consent to application")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: Radware says exposed Cloud WAF management API let attackers obtain customer account details and cloud access keys

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, Radware has disclosed that attackers accessed some customers' account details and cloud access keys. Radware attributes the breach to an unsecured internal Cloud WAF management API that had been left reachable from the internet. The report, published 24 November 2026, does not say how many customers were affected, which keys or cloud platforms were involved, or when the access happened.
writeup.why_it_matters: Organizations that use Radware Cloud WAF may hold credentials that attackers now have, and those keys can be used to change WAF policy or reach linked cloud resources without touching any endpoint. Radware confirms the access took place, so treat any Radware-related keys as compromised until Radware says otherwise. The current reporting rests on a single source and leaves out scope details, so confirm your own exposure directly with Radware.
recommended_actions: Contact Radware to confirm whether your tenant's account details or access keys were among those exposed.
Rotate all API keys, access keys and credentials tied to Radware Cloud WAF. Revoke any cloud provider access keys that were ever shared with Radware.
Review Radware Cloud WAF audit logs for unexpected policy, origin, certificate or user changes. Check cloud provider logs for activity using the rotated keys.
Reset passwords and enforce MFA on Radware portal accounts, and watch for phishing that pretends to be Radware breach notifications.
Restrict any cloud credentials used by third-party security services to least privilege, and limit them to known source IP ranges where the provider supports it.

sources.title: Radware discloses breach exposing customer cloud access keys

hunting_steps: Inventory every credential your organization has issued to Radware: Cloud WAF API keys, portal accounts, and any AWS, Azure or GCP keys used for integration.
Pull the Radware Cloud WAF audit trail for recent configuration changes, such as security policy relaxation, origin server changes, new users or new API tokens, and confirm each with its owner.
In cloud provider logs, search for calls made with Radware-associated access keys from unfamiliar IP addresses, regions or user agents, especially enumeration or IAM changes.
If Defender for Cloud Apps connects AWS, use CloudAppEvents to review activity tied to the integration identity and look for new IAM users or keys.
After rotation, confirm the old keys are disabled and that no failed or successful calls still use them.

hunting_queries.title: AWS IAM and key changes seen via Defender for Cloud Apps
hunting_queries.kql:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| where ActionType in~ ("CreateAccessKey", "CreateUser", "AttachUserPolicy", "PutUserPolicy", "CreateLoginProfile", "UpdateAccessKey")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: AWS activity from new countries by account in last 7 days
hunting_queries.kql:
let baseline = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp between (ago(37d) .. ago(7d))
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| summarize KnownCountries = make_set(CountryCode) by AccountDisplayName;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Amazon Web Services"
| join kind=leftouter baseline on AccountDisplayName
| where isnull(KnownCountries) or not(set_has_element(KnownCountries, CountryCode))
| summarize Events = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20) by AccountDisplayName, CountryCode
| order by Events desc

stories.title: Turnitin discloses unauthorized activity on certain customer-facing systems

writeup.what_happened: According to BleepingComputer, Turnitin CEO Chris Caren said in a statement that the company recently detected unauthorized activity involving certain customer-facing systems. The available reporting does not say how the attacker got in, which systems or data were involved, when the activity began, or whether customer credentials or integrations were exposed. The sources name no CVE, malware or indicators.
writeup.why_it_matters: Many universities and schools connect Turnitin to learning management systems and single sign-on, so a compromise of its customer-facing systems could expose user data or integration secrets held by those organizations. With no technical details yet, the practical risk for defenders is follow-on phishing that uses Turnitin branding and possible misuse of integration credentials. Do nothing drastic now, but watch for further vendor disclosures.
recommended_actions: Find out whether your organization uses Turnitin, and which identity and LMS integrations it relies on (SSO apps, LTI keys, API tokens).
Contact Turnitin for scoping details and any customer guidance, and follow vendor notifications as the investigation continues.
Rotate Turnitin API keys, LTI shared secrets or service account credentials if Turnitin confirms that integration data was exposed.
Warn users and help desk staff about phishing that uses Turnitin branding or refers to the incident.

stories.title: Unit 42 tracks intrusion campaigns run by autonomous AI agents

writeup.what_happened: Unit 42 reports that it has tracked campaigns in which attackers used autonomous AI agents to automate intrusions across multiple platforms. According to Unit 42, the agents relied on standard tools but left distinctive operational traces. The available summary gives no victims, timeframes, specific tools, indicators or technical traces, so the scope and methods cannot be confirmed from this source alone.
writeup.why_it_matters: If Unit 42's findings hold, attackers can run intrusion steps faster and at greater scale, and much of that activity may look like ordinary administrative tool use on Windows, cloud and edge systems. No CVE, product or indicator is tied to this report, so defenders have nothing specific to patch or block yet. The practical value lies in the operational traces Unit 42 describes in its full write-up.
recommended_actions: Read the full Unit 42 report and pull out any concrete behaviors, tools or indicators it documents for detection engineering.

Review existing detections for built-in and dual-use tool abuse (discovery commands, remote execution, credential access) to confirm they fire on activity that is fast and scripted, not only on manual operator activity.
Make sure alerting covers bursts of reconnaissance and lateral movement from a single account or host within short time windows, because automated agents tend to compress intrusion timelines.

stories.title: Four command injection flaws in Panabit Smart Application Gateway TANGr7p10, no vendor fix

writeup.what_happened: NVD published four CVEs on 24 November 2026 for Panabit Smart Application Gateway TANGr7p10: OS command injection in the dashboard chart dump endpoint (CVE-2026-135790), the flow control pie chart function (CVE-2026-135791), and the email auth code sender in user.cgi through the Username argument (CVE-2026-135792, CVSS 9.3), plus code injection in the SAC crontab function through the cmd argument (CVE-2026-135794). According to the NVD descriptions, all four can be triggered remotely and exploit details are public. The disclosures say Panabit was contacted early and did not respond, and no patch is mentioned. Automated proof-of-concept tracking did not confirm public exploit code, so the sources disagree on how available working exploits are.
writeup.why_it_matters: Panabit gateways are niche outside China, but any exposed unit is an edge device where command injection means control of a traffic chokepoint. None of the CVEs are in CISA KEV, and EPSS is modest (0.6% to 2.3%). With public exploit details and no vendor fix, exposure reduction is the only real defense. CVE-2026-135792 sits in a user-facing authentication function, so it may be reachable without admin access, though the sources do not state whether authentication is required.
recommended_actions: Inventory Panabit Smart Application Gateway devices, and confirm whether any web management or user portal interfaces are reachable from the internet.
Restrict management and portal access to trusted administrative networks or a VPN until Panabit releases a fix.

Review gateway web and system logs for requests to ajax_chart_dump, ajax_data_pie, user.cgi send_email_authcode and ajax_sac_crontab that contain shell metacharacters, and check for unexpected crontab entries.
Watch for unusual outbound connections from gateway management IPs, such as callbacks or downloads, that could indicate compromise.
Contact Panabit or your reseller for patch status, and consider replacing exposed units if no fix arrives.

hunting_steps: Identify Panabit gateways in asset inventories and external attack surface scans, and record their management IP addresses.
Check whether the gateway web interfaces are internet-facing, and restrict them if they are.
Search managed endpoints for browser or tool connections to the vulnerable CGI endpoints, to find admin workstations and any unexpected internal sources.
Pull the gateway's own web logs, if available, and look for vulnerable endpoint requests with characters such as semicolons, pipes, backticks or $( in parameters.
Inspect the device's scheduled tasks or crontab for entries an administrator did not create.
Review firewall logs for outbound connections that originate from gateway management addresses.

hunting_queries.title: Endpoint connections to vulnerable Panabit CGI endpoints
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has_any ("ajax_chart_dump", "ajax_data_pie", "send_email_authcode", "ajax_sac_crontab") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Command lines referencing Panabit vulnerable endpoints
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ajax_chart_dump", "ajax_data_pie", "send_email_authcode", "ajax_sac_crontab") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName | order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: Two command injection flaws in Volans NGFW r5.1 disclosed with no vendor response

writeup.what_happened: NVD published two OS command injection vulnerabilities in the Volans NGFW Next-Generation Firewall r5.1 on 24 November 2026. CVE-2026-135796 (CVSS 8.6) affects a port scan module in the Web Management UI, and CVE-2026-135797 (CVSS 9.3) affects the SSLVPN Client component. Both can be triggered remotely. According to NVD, exploit details have been publicly disclosed and the vendor did not respond when contacted before disclosure, so no fix is known.
writeup.why_it_matters: If you run Volans NGFW with the SSL VPN or management interface reachable from untrusted networks, an attacker could execute OS commands on the firewall and use it to reach internal systems. Neither CVE is in CISA KEV and EPSS is low (2.5% and 2.3%). The sources disagree on exploit availability: NVD says it is public, while separate tracking found no public proof-of-concept code. With no vendor patch, mitigation depends on reducing exposure.
recommended_actions: Identify any Volans NGFW appliances in your estate, including those run by third parties or branch offices, and confirm their versions.
Restrict the Web Management UI to a dedicated management network or allowlisted administrator IPs, and never expose it to the internet.
If the SSL VPN is not required, disable it. If it is required, limit access by source IP where possible and plan to move to a supported VPN solution, since the vendor has not responded.
Review appliance logs for unusual requests to the SSL VPN client and management endpoints, unexpected configuration changes, and new administrator accounts.
Monitor traffic originating from the firewall itself for unexpected outbound connections or internal scanning, which could indicate compromise.

hunting_steps: Inventory Volans NGFW appliances and record which ones expose the management UI or SSL VPN to the internet.
Check vulnerability management data for either CVE. Coverage for this niche vendor may be absent, so rely on the asset inventory as well.
In firewall and proxy logs, review requests to the SSL VPN client path and management UI from unfamiliar external sources.
Look for connections from firewall management or internal interface IPs to internal hosts on admin ports (SMB, RDP, WinRM, SSH) that do not match normal behavior.

If you suspect compromise, take a configuration backup, compare it against a known-good baseline, and rotate credentials stored on or authenticated through the device, such as VPN users and LDAP bind accounts.

hunting_queries.title: Devices with Volans NGFW CVEs in Defender vulnerability management
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities | where CveId in ("CVE-2026-135796", "CVE-2026-135797") | project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel

explainer.concept: Forged tokens from stolen signing keys: why one private key can be every admin
explainer.dek: When an identity service signs authentication tokens with a private key, anyone who steals that key can mint valid tokens for any user, with no password, MFA or login event.
explainer.why_today: Rapid7's vCenter chain did not stop at the authentication bypass: it copied the directory database, took the STS signing key and forged an administrator session. That last step explains why patching alone does not undo a compromise.

parts.heading: How token signing works
paragraphs: Federated and single sign-on systems do not re-check a password every time a user reaches a service. A token service authenticates the user once, then issues a signed assertion, such as a SAML token, saying who the user is and what groups they belong to. Relying services check the signature against a certificate they trust and accept the claims inside.

In vCenter, the vSphere SSO Secure Token Service (STS) issues these tokens, and its signing material lives in the VMware Directory Service. In Microsoft environments, AD FS signs SAML tokens with its token-signing certificate, and Entra ID trusts that certificate for federated domains. The design is the same in both: the signing key is the root of trust for every session.

parts.heading: What an attacker gains
paragraphs: With the private key, an attacker can write a token for any identity, including built-in administrators, add any group claims, and sign it so the relying service accepts it. This is the technique publicly described as Golden SAML. It was used against AD FS in the SolarWinds-era intrusions.

Forged tokens skip the identity provider's login. No password is checked, MFA is never prompted, and conditional checks that run at the identity provider may never fire. The key stays valid until it is replaced. Patching the bug that exposed it, or resetting user passwords, does not invalidate tokens the attacker can keep minting.

parts.heading: What it looks like in telemetry
paragraphs: The forged sign-in itself often looks normal to the relying service. Look for the gap instead: a session at the service with no matching authentication event at the token issuer. For AD FS-federated Entra ID tenants, that means federated sign-ins in Entra logs without corresponding AD FS token issuance events. Defender for Identity can also alert on suspicious reads of the AD FS key material in Active Directory.

On vCenter, the forged session is usually followed by noisier actions. Watch for new local SSO or superAdmin-type accounts, SSH or the shell being enabled on the appliance, unexpected access to or export of the directory database, and administrative logins from unfamiliar sources. Forward vCenter and appliance logs to Sentinel so these events survive an attacker with root.

parts.heading: Recovery and prevention
paragraphs: If a signing key may have been exposed, treat it as burned. Replace the STS signing certificate using VMware's documented certificate replacement procedure. For AD FS, Microsoft's compromise guidance calls for rolling the token-signing certificate twice, so the previous certificate cannot be reused. Then remove persistence the attacker created with their forged access.

Prevention means treating token issuers as tier-zero. Restrict network reach to their management and directory ports, limit who can log in, and monitor key access. Where it fits, reduce dependence on on-premises federation, for example by moving Entra ID domains from AD FS to cloud authentication.

takeaways: If any vCenter was reachable on TCP 2012 before patching for CVE-2026-123890, assume the STS signing key may be exposed. Replace it following VMware's guidance after patching.
Audit vCenter for SSO or local accounts created recently, SSH or shell enablement, and admin logins from unexpected hosts. Send those logs to Sentinel.
In Sentinel, correlate Entra ID federated sign-ins with AD FS token issuance events and alert on sign-ins that have no matching issuance.
Confirm Defender for Identity sensors are deployed on AD FS servers and review any alerts about AD FS key material access.
Inventory every system whose signing key can mint admin sessions, such as AD FS, vCenter STS and other SSO providers. Restrict network access to them as tier-zero assets.

good_news.headline: Unit 42 publishes analysis and patch guidance for NGINX HTTP/2 use-after-free CVE-2026-123633
good_news.summary: Unit 42 published a technical analysis of CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 handling. According to Unit 42, the write-up covers affected versions, sanitizer testing and patch guidance, giving defenders what they need to scope exposure and prioritize updates.

good_news.headline: Microsoft confirms Visio remote code execution flaw was fixed in November 2026 updates
good_news.summary: According to the MSRC Security Update Guide, CVE-2026-112732, a Microsoft Office Visio remote code execution vulnerability, was addressed by updates released in November 2026 but was left out of that month's security update listing. Microsoft says customers who have already installed the November 2026 updates need to take no further action.

good_news.headline: Schneider Electric provides remediations for EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody memory flaws
good_news.summary: A CISA advisory says Schneider Electric has published remediations for a vulnerability in EcoStruxure Power Build Rapsody, its switchboard design software. According to the advisory, the flaw could cause memory corruption and heap- or stack-based buffer overflows if left unremediated.
